claims.text: A PostgreSQL standby (PostgreSQL's name for a server following a primary; here the read replica) receives the primary's changes as a stream and applies them; with hot standby it answers read-only queries.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: 26.2.5 Streaming Replication; 26.4 Hot Standby

claims.text: A hot standby refuses every write: data-modifying statements fail with 'cannot execute UPDATE in a read-only transaction', since all its transactions are read-only.
Streaming replication is asynchronous by default (synchronous_standby_names empty): the primary commits without waiting for any standby to receive or apply the change.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: 26.2.5 Streaming Replication ('asynchronous by default'); 26.2.8 Synchronous Replication; 19.6.2 synchronous_standby_names

claims.text: With async replication a change becomes visible on the standby after a delay, typically under a second while it keeps up with the load; no limit is promised, and a standby that cannot keep up falls further behind. Commit visibility on one server does not cover a second server.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: 26.2.5 Streaming Replication (delay typically under one second); 26.4.1 Hot Standby User's Overview (measurable delay; differing results)

claims.text: A standby built with pg_basebackup starts as a copy of the whole primary server (all databases, tables and rows), as db/replica/start.sh does; the compose comment says it copies db once, then streams db's changes.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: pg_basebackup reference; 26.2.4 Setting Up a Standby Server; examples/don-hang @ stage-3 docker-compose.yml lines 581-585, db/replica/start.sh

claims.text: All writes go to the single primary; each standby replays the same changes. Replicas add read capacity only; write capacity stays that of one server.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: 26.1 Comparison of Different Solutions (primary/standby, only the primary accepts writes); 26.4 Hot Standby

claims.text: Reads that follow the caller's own write (e.g. the order just placed) cannot go to a lagging replica; sending them to the primary is one simple way to keep read-your-writes. Reads that tolerate data a few seconds old (e.g. product list) may go to a replica.
claims.source_hint: Condition stated in text (whether the read follows its own write and tolerates stale data); general replication design guidance

claims.text: pg_is_in_recovery() returns true while the server is in recovery, which is the case on a standby replaying changes from the primary.

A service with profiles: [...] is not started by a plain docker compose up; it starts only when one of its profiles is enabled (--profile replica).
